items.title: Grant Thornton warns AI audits could become a race to the bottom
items.summary: Grant Thornton's UK head of audit warned that firms competing to deliver the fastest and cheapest AI-driven audit could erode audit quality.
detail: The comments, reported on 23 November, come days after KPMG ran a pilot audit of a FTSE 250 company using more than 100 AI agents.

The warning adds to a wider debate in the UK profession about how far AI can take over audit fieldwork while firms still carry responsibility for the opinion. UK commentary has already stressed that auditors cannot blame AI tools for audit failures.
items.why: A live example of the audit quality and professional scepticism questions that come up in auditing and ethics units.

items.title: ASIC logs hundreds of audit complaints against the Big Four
items.summary: Australia's corporate regulator has recorded 558 audit complaints against the Big Four firms, with Deloitte attracting the most.
detail: According to Capital Brief, Deloitte accounted for 260 complaints made to ASIC and 1,206 internal complaints. ASIC says some matters are being considered for enforcement, and KPMG is already under investigation over misstatements in its transparency reporting.

The figure updates ASIC's September count of 551 complaints. ASIC began this surveillance of the firms' internal complaints in July 2023, and its October surveillance report named large audit firms alongside its findings and asked the Big Four, BDO and Grant Thornton for action plans.

The scrutiny follows the KPMG whistleblower affair earlier this year, which led to the departure of its CEO, chairman and head of audit, and government comments that it is considering breaking up the Big Four.
items.why: Directly relevant to Australian audit regulation and the AASB/ASIC reporting environment you study in Melbourne.

items.title: Nvidia drops about 8% as doubts grow over Huang's return
items.summary: Nvidia gave back much of Monday's 31% surge as lawmakers from both parties questioned the circumstances of Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.
detail: Nvidia shares fell about 8% on Tuesday after jumping more than 30% on Monday when the board brought Huang back. Huang had resigned on 12 November over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

Lawmakers said Congress should scrutinise his return, and reports raised questions about President Trump's role. The board has formed committees on possible foreign intelligence targeting and on national security and export controls. Huang faces a closed-door hearing before three House committees on 1 December and a livestreamed Senate hearing on 3 December.
items.why: A rare case study in board governance, CEO succession and how governance risk feeds straight into market value.

items.title: Wall Street splits as chip stocks fall and the Dow rises
items.summary: The Dow gained while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell on Tuesday as chip stocks slid and a report said the US is preparing new tariffs.
detail: By mid-morning on the US West Coast the S&P 500 was about 0.5% lower at 7,197.83 while the Dow was up about 0.75% at 49,969.57, with Nvidia and AMD sharply lower. Later reports put the S&P 500's fall at 1.1% to 1.3%; the final close was not yet confirmed at the time of writing.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the US is preparing tariffs on China, the EU and 14 other countries. The Conference Board consumer confidence index rose to 103.3 in November from 91.9, against an estimate of 92.5, and the 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.89%.
items.why: Shows how tariff news, rate expectations and one mega-cap stock can move index returns in a single session.

items.title: ASX 200 snaps an eight-day losing streak
items.summary: The ASX 200 rose 1.82% to 8,726.4 on Tuesday, its first gain after eight straight falls.
detail: The index added 155.8 points from Monday's close of 8,570.6. The previous eight sessions had taken about 6.4% off the market.
The rally followed Monday's tech rebound on Wall Street after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang. Ten of the eleven sectors closed higher, with energy the only sector in the red.
items.why: Local market context for any Australian valuation or portfolio work this week.

items.title: ATO sets out how it will run Division 296 for SMSFs
items.summary: The ATO has explained the process for assessing the new Division 296 tax on large superannuation balances for self-managed super funds.
detail: The process applies from the 2028 financial year. The ATO will change the 2027 SMSF annual return to capture the earnings it needs for the calculation.
Once the ATO issues its notifications, the Division 296 liability will be due and payable 84 days later.
items.why: Division 296 is one of the biggest recent changes to Australian tax on super and a likely topic in Australian tax units.

items.title: Malaysian MPs press the government on global minimum tax results
items.summary: Malaysia's Dewan Rakyat was set to question the finance minister on how much the global minimum tax has raised since 2025.
detail: Bernama reported on 23 November that MPs would ask about revenue from the global minimum tax since its 2025 start and whether micro, small and medium enterprises could receive a 15% rate. The rapid growth of data centres was also on the agenda.

The global minimum tax requires large multinationals with group revenue of at least €750 million to pay a 15% effective rate. The current sitting runs until 8 December, so the minister's answers may follow.
items.why: An ASEAN neighbour of Indonesia testing what Pillar Two has actually delivered, a useful comparison for Indonesia's own GloBE rules.

items.title: Costa revives an EU digital levy and Ireland pushes back
items.summary: European Council president António Costa has put an EU-wide digital levy back on the table in budget talks, and Ireland's Taoiseach has rejected it.
detail: The Irish Times reported on 21 November that the proposal would be a 3% charge on revenues from online advertising, digital marketplaces and the monetisation of user data, raised as an own resource for the EU budget.
The Taoiseach argued that part of the earlier global tax agreement was that there would be no digital tax. Any EU-wide tax would need unanimous support from member states.
items.why: Shows how the Pillar One deal's promise to remove digital services taxes is under strain.

items.title: IHSG edges up 0.49% as MSCI holds firm on downgrade plan
items.summary: IHSG closed at 5,241.58 on Tuesday after a volatile session, as MSCI said there would be no compromise on its plan to move Indonesia to standalone market status.
detail: The index rose 25.73 points from 5,215.85 and traded between 5,198.64 and 5,314.74. Financials, consumer staples and infrastructure stocks led, and LQ45 rose 1.10% to 546.13. IHSG had been up as much as 1.82% in the morning before MSCI's statement trimmed the gain.

MSCI opened a consultation on 15 October on moving Indonesia from Emerging Market to Standalone status, citing concerns over opaque ownership and coordinated trading. Despite two days of gains, IHSG is still down 1.19% from its 17 November close of 5,304.76.
items.why: The MSCI case puts free float, ownership transparency and OJK/BEI market governance at the centre of Indonesian capital market policy.

items.title: Rupiah slips to Rp18,230 on MSCI worries
items.summary: The spot rupiah closed 0.15% weaker at Rp18,230 per US dollar on Tuesday, while BI's JISDOR reference rate firmed 0.10% to Rp18,204.
detail: The rupiah gave up 27 points from Monday's Rp18,203 after trading near Rp18,199 in the morning. Kontan linked the fall to investor concern over MSCI's demands for stronger market supervision and clear rules on high shareholding concentration, plus a firmer US dollar against Asian currencies.
Analyst Ibrahim Assuaibi expects the rupiah to stay volatile on Wednesday and possibly close weaker in a range of Rp18,230 to Rp18,280.
items.why: Exchange rates drive Indonesian tax translation (kurs pajak) and PSAK 10 foreign currency reporting.

items.title: DJP pushes PPh 25 instalment adjustments to close the revenue gap
items.summary: DJP will adjust (dinamisasi) PPh Pasal 25 instalments for the November and December 2026 periods, with about Rp560.9 trillion still needed to meet the 2026 target.
detail: DJP says the aim is to make instalments match businesses' actual 2026 conditions. Under Article 120(1) of PER-11/PJ/2025, DJP may raise instalments when the tax expected to be owed exceeds 125% of the base used to set them.

An economist quoted by Jawa Pos estimates receipts must average about Rp257 trillion a month in November and December, well above the roughly Rp180 trillion monthly average from January to October. Critics often call the practice ijon pajak, meaning tax collected in advance.
items.why: A practical example of how instalment rules and year-end collection pressure shape Indonesian taxpayer cash flow and disputes.

items.title: PMK 55/2026 tightens tax consultant licensing
items.summary: Anyone working as a tax consultant in Indonesia must hold a licence under PMK 55/2026, and incomplete applications lapse after 30 working days.
detail: DDTCNews explains that Article 3 of PMK 55/2026 makes a licence compulsory for practising as a tax consultant.
Applicants must supply any requested documents within a maximum of 30 working days, or the application is treated as not submitted.
items.why: Relevant if you plan to work in Indonesian tax practice after your degree.
